prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots placed GLP-1 first, and I still hold that this is justified on the merits and not only on the vote count. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through identification of the active truncated peptide and its physiology, to long-acting agonists with demonstrated cardiovascular, renal and weight benefit is complete and independently replicated, with decades of randomized outcome data. The discovery content (Holst on native physiology, Drucker on receptor and tissue biology and translation, Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active form) fits a three-person prize built around discovery, and the medical impact is among the largest of any candidate on the shortlist. Recognition is timely.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for identification of the active peptide is disputed (Mojsov, Habener and others), and a three-person cap leaves out Knudsen, whose medicinal chemistry produced liraglutide and semaglutide, the drugs that carried the biology to patients. A prize that honours the discovery while omitting the drug design may look incomplete to the public, and one that includes Knudsen at Mojsov's expense forces the committee to judge a priority dispute I cannot resolve from the file. There is also a risk that unanimity at the opening stage reflects shared recollection of a well-known story and not verified history.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that this trio covers discovery, physiology and drug development, and that Mojsov must be dropped under the three-person cap.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously, since Knudsen's contribution is real and the translation is the reason this prize case is so strong. However, the prize is for a discovery, and the physiology credit is thinner with Mojsov removed: the identification and synthesis of the active form of the peptide is what made the rest of the work possible. Industrial drug optimization by a company team builds on that, and I would rather separate it than let it displace a discovery credit. I would not object strongly to the Linnarsson trio if the committee judges Mojsov's priority too uncertain, so I regard this as a close call and not a firm disagreement.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked CAR-T second and treated GLP-1 and CAR-T as the two most clearly transformative therapeutic stories, noting that Eshhar and others are missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that CAR-T is the strongest challenger and I ranked it second myself. Where I differ is on how settled it is. The credit problem for first-generation chimeric receptors (Eshhar and others) is a real gap for the supplied names, and Rosenberg's contribution is mostly an adoptive-therapy lineage and not CAR-specific, so the three-person configuration is less secure than GLP-1. Long-term toxicity and secondary malignancy are also still being characterized. I would see CAR-T as a very good candidate for a later year or as a second part only if the committee found a way to share the prize, which the three-person cap makes awkward.

responses.point: Svenningsson placed GLP-1 first with the same Drucker, Holst, Mojsov trio, and was cautious about Sabatini in the TOR candidate because of documented conduct concerns, and about optogenetics because its medical benefit is still limited.
responses.response: I agree on the GLP-1 trio, and I take the point that optogenetics fits the medical mandate less well than a therapy-linked discovery. On Sabatini I would be careful: the conduct question is separate from the scientific credit and should not drive the committee's attribution judgment without verified facts, though it may reasonably affect whether the committee wants to prize TOR this year. That is another reason I prefer to concentrate the debate on candidates with cleaner attribution. I would not use TOR as a fallback.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked the unfolded protein response second and described it as a clean two-person mechanistic prize with stable attribution.
responses.response: I agree that Walter and Mori are a clean pair and that the mechanism is textbook. My hesitation is the medical weight: the link to disease is indirect and clinical translation is still early, whereas GLP-1 shows the whole arc to patient benefit. I would keep the unfolded protein response as a strong alternative or a later-year candidate, and I would not prefer it over GLP-1 or CAR-T this year, even though the attribution is simpler.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should credit the identification of the active peptide (Mojsov) or the drug design (Knudsen) as the third name; I cannot verify the priority history from the file.
Whether other early contributors outside the credited list, such as Habener, make any three-person GLP-1 configuration unfair.
Whether two distinct achievements sharing the prize, for example GLP-1 with CAR-T, would be workable under the three-person cap without splitting the GLP-1 credit.
Whether the CAR-T attribution gap (Eshhar and others) can be resolved enough to make it a serious competitor this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for GLP-1, CAR-T or the unfolded protein response. My research is in autoimmunity (Sjogren's disease, lupus, Ro52/TRIM21), and the field of CAR-T in autoimmunity is adjacent but I have no documented involvement with the credited individuals. My Bergen group-leader affiliation and past co-authors (Kuchroo, Sonesson) do not connect to any shortlisted candidate.
